en: Serious burn injuries that need careful cooling and urgent medical help.
A path that pedestrians and cyclists may both use.
A curve in the road that turns tightly and may need a clear speed reduction.
A serious medical condition after injury when the body is not circulating blood well.
Looking over your shoulder to see areas the mirrors may miss.
A smaller road that joins a main road.
Strong wind blowing across the road from the side, which can push a vehicle off its line.
A one-wheeled passenger compartment fixed to the side of a motorcycle.
Small, low-power lights used to make a parked or moving vehicle more visible.
Low-power front and rear position lights; not bright enough alone for driving at speed.
Cuts or damage in the side wall of a tyre that can make it illegal or unsafe.
The person who controls railway signals and barriers at a level crossing.
Using indicators (or other signals) to show other road users what you intend to do.
A road without a central reservation separating opposite directions of traffic.
A road without a central reservation separating opposite directions of traffic.
A narrow road wide enough for only one vehicle, so drivers may need to wait to pass.
Marks left on the road when tyres lose grip; on warning signs they often mean a slippery road ahead.
When tyres lose grip and the vehicle slides instead of staying under control.
The short linking road used to join or leave a motorway.
A road surface with poor tyre grip, so vehicles can skid more easily.
A road surface with poor grip, so vehicles can skid more easily.
A warning that the road surface may be slippery.
A road that is wet, icy, or otherwise hard for tyres to grip.
Metal chains fitted around tyres to improve grip in deep snow or ice.
A vehicle that clears snow from the road, often with a blade at the front.
An unbroken white road marking that often means you must not cross or enter.
A declaration that a vehicle is kept off public roads and is not taxed for road use.
Using the vehicle horn to make a warning sound.
A camera that records vehicles breaking the speed limit.
An area where cameras check vehicle speeds for enforcement.
Cameras that detect vehicles exceeding the speed limit.
A raised ridge across the road that forces drivers to slow down.
Raised ridges across the road that force drivers to slow down (also called sleeping policemen).
Raised sections across the road designed to slow traffic down.
Devices that restrict how fast a large vehicle can go, often required by law for lorries.
Water thrown up by tyres on a wet road that reduces how far you can see.
A device that helps reduce swaying of a trailer or caravan while towing.
A device that reduces unwanted swinging or swaying of a trailer while towing.
A junction where side roads join from left and right at slightly different points, not opposite each other.
The engine stops unexpectedly, often when starting or changing gear.
Not moving; the vehicle is at a complete stop.
Vehicles that have stopped and are not moving, often in a queue.
A sharp slope going downwards where speed can increase quickly.
A sharp uphill climb where the road rises quickly.
A security lock that stops the steering wheel turning when the key is removed.
Shaking felt through the steering wheel while driving.
The solid white line at a junction that marks where you must stop when required.
The total distance needed to stop: thinking distance plus braking distance.
How long you have to react and brake before you would hit the vehicle ahead.
Drive with wheels on both sides of a line, partly crossing it.
Raised reflective road markers that help show where lanes and edges are, especially at night.
Small rectangular signs placed under a main road sign that add details such as times or exceptions.
The springs and related parts that connect the wheels to the car body and absorb bumps.
Side-to-side swinging of a trailer or caravan while being towed, which can become dangerous.
A sudden change of direction to avoid something, such as a pothole or slippery patch.
Suddenly changing direction, often to avoid something in the road.
Moves out to the right before turning left—common for long vehicles that need more space.
A junction where one road meets another and ends, forming a ‘T’ shape.
The red lights at the rear of a vehicle that show its position to drivers behind.
Paying UK vehicle tax (VED) so the vehicle can be used on public roads.
A short-term alternative route when the normal road cannot be used.
Short-term alternative routes when the normal road is closed or blocked.
One or more lanes closed for a limited time, often during road works.
Something briefly blocking or slowing traffic, such as a stopped vehicle.
Short-term construction or repairs that change normal road conditions.
A speed limit that applies only for a limited time, often near roadworks.
Portable signals used for a limited time, often at road works.
Insurance that covers injury/damage to others, plus fire damage and theft of your vehicle.
A motorway with three lanes in each direction of travel.
A belt that keeps engine valves and pistons moving in the correct timing.
Lenses that are darkened or coloured, reducing how much light reaches your eyes.
A metric unit of weight used on UK restriction signs for heavy vehicles.
Places of interest for visitors, such as landmarks or museums.
The ball-shaped coupling on a tow bar that the trailer hitch locks onto.
The metal bar fitted to a vehicle for attaching and towing a trailer or caravan.
A caravan being pulled behind another vehicle on the road.
Pulling a trailer, caravan, or another vehicle behind your car using a tow bar or hitch.
Pulling a trailer attached behind your vehicle.
A slow agricultural vehicle often seen on country roads; overtaking needs clear space and time.
Road features designed to slow vehicles down, such as humps or narrowings.
An official authorised to manage traffic on motorways and some major roads.
Specialist road staff who manage incidents and traffic on motorways and major A-roads.
Road features such as humps or narrowings designed to keep vehicle speeds lower.
An unpowered wheeled unit designed to be towed behind a vehicle to carry loads.
Electric passenger vehicles that run on rails set into the road surface.
The system that transfers engine power to the wheels, including the gearbox.
Lines painted across the road (often yellow) to alert you as you approach a hazard.
Yellow lines painted across the road (from side to side), not along it.
How deep the grooves in a tyre are; worn-down tread reduces grip, especially in wet weather.
A red-bordered triangle road sign that warns of a hazard ahead.
A road passage that goes under ground or through a hill.
A rule of thumb: stay at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead in good, dry conditions.
In good, dry conditions, keep at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead.
A road where traffic travels in both directions.
Roads where traffic travels in both directions.
Traffic moving in both directions on the same road.
How well the tyres hold the road surface for steering and braking.
How well the tyres hold onto the road surface without sliding.
How much air is in each tyre; incorrect pressure affects handling, braking, and tyre wear.
How much air is in each tyre; incorrect pressure affects handling, braking, and tyre wear.
How the tyre rubber wears down; uneven wear can signal a fault.
Tyres with too little air; can raise fuel use and affect braking.
Turning the vehicle all the way round to go back the way you came.
Turning the vehicle around in a U-shape to go back the way you came.
Left alone with no one in or watching the vehicle.
A trailer without its own brakes; coupling safety devices are especially important.
Not awake and not responding; may need emergency help.
Tyres with too little air pressure, which can worsen handling and wear.
A road that is bumpy or irregular rather than smooth.
A bumpy or irregular road that can affect control and comfort.
A road with no street lighting at night.
A junction where roads meet with no give-way or stop signs or road markings.
A section of road going up a slope.
An urban road where stopping is restricted during posted times, except briefly for passengers.
Air and noise pollution in towns and cities, often from traffic.
Electronic signs that change to show live warnings or instructions.
Temporary speed limits shown on overhead signs that change with traffic conditions.
Who legally owns the vehicle; changes of ownership must be recorded with the DVLA.
The official number plate details that identify a vehicle.
Another name for the V5C registration document showing vehicle and keeper details.
The V5C paper that records the vehicle’s details and its registered keeper.
The official paper (V5C / log book) that records who the vehicle is registered to.
The UK road tax (VED) you must pay to use a vehicle on public roads.
The soft or grassy edge beside the road, not meant for normal driving.
UK phrase meaning you can see only a short distance, often under about 100 metres.
More at risk of injury in a collision because of little physical protection (e.g. bikes, motorcycles, pedestrians).
Rules that limit when you may wait or park along a stretch of road.
A parking or traffic warden who enforces parking rules.
A red reflective triangle placed on the road to warn others of a broken-down vehicle.
Water collecting in low spots on the road after rain.
When drive wheels spin too fast on a slippery surface and lose grip.
A road with many bends, where overtaking is often difficult and slow traffic can build up.
The upright frames at the edges of the windscreen that can block part of your view.
A cone-shaped cloth tube that shows wind direction and strength; used as a road-sign symbol.
Yellow road markings at the kerb that restrict waiting or parking.
A pedestrian crossing with black-and-white stripes where drivers must give way to people waiting to cross.
A pedestrian crossing with black-and-white stripes where drivers must give way to people waiting to cross.
Yellow zig-zag lines near crossings or schools where you must not park or stop and block the view.
Zigzag road markings near crossings; parking and waiting there is restricted.
